#2027. Man United set to appoint Mauricio Pochettino as head coach: Club make formal approach to US Soccer after agreeing personal terms - with Michael Carrick's exit confirmed on Thursday

Published: 03:10 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 12:15 EST, 12 November 2026

Manchester United are set to name Mauricio Pochettino as head coach to replace Michael Carrick following a day of talks over both men.

United moved closer to putting Pochettino in charge at Old Trafford after reaching a verbal agreement with the US national team boss on Wednesday. The club then made a formal approach to US Soccer.

Meanwhile, the club’s chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox flew back from Monaco, where minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe was expected to ratify their decision to sack Carrick with the blessing of co-chairmen Joel and Avram Glazer.

Carrick’s departure could be confirmed on Thursday, but official confirmation of Pochettino’s appointment may take a little longer with more talks planned overnight on Wednesday.

Pochettino is currently at the US Soccer base outside Atlanta preparing for a CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final double header against Haiti, and is due to speak to the media on Friday.

It’s unclear if he will remain in charge for those games, with United said to be relaxed over the Argentine taking the team. It is possible he could stay for the first leg in Kingston, Jamaica at the weekend and then travel to Manchester.

Manchester United are set to name Mauricio Pochettino as their new manager - but he took training as usual on Wednesday

Pochettino, who has managed Southampton,Tottenham, and Chelsea, will succeed Michael Carrick

Carrick checked in at Carrington at 7.45am on Wednesday with his fate in the balance

He was pictured leaving Manchester United's training base at around 1.15pm

Pochettino is pictured working on United States national team duty on Tuesday (Source: X/USMNT)

The second leg is Cincinnati is not until the early hours of Thursday, and Pochettino may even would only take over at United on Friday with a huge game against Liverpool at Anfield 48 hours later.

It’s understood that the US Soccer Federation are ready for this contingency and have a succession plan in place should he leave.

It will cost Pochettino around £7million to buy himself out of his contract with the US Soccer Federation, with United ready to foot the bill.

The cost of bringing in his back-room team, including trusted assistants Jesus Perez and Miguel D’Agostino, will take the cost above £10m.

The 54-year-old only signed a new deal after the World Cup meaning that United could have got him for nothing in the summer.

Amid the secret talks between United and Pochettino’s camp on Wednesday, there was more intrigue when the federation cancelled media access to the players at late notice but allowed cameras to film an open training session.

Sources said the decision was made out of respect for Veterans Day in America, but it also meant the players didn’t have to field any awkward questions over their coach’s future.

Bournemouth midfielder Tyler Adams was quoted by the US media as saying: ‘Why would his name not be on it (United’s list)?

Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox are meeting in Monaco for talks today

The United execs meet in Monaco today (Pictured is the Casino Monte-Carlo in Monaco)

‘I mean, the credibility, the resume speaks for itself. It goes to show for us how lucky we are to be able to work under a manager of his quality and the person he is.’

Meanwhile, Berrada and Wilcox flew back to Manchester from Nice on Wednesday with United expected to announce Carrick’s departure imminently after 10 months in charge.

The 45-year-old took training at Carrington for the second day running, arriving at 7.45am and leaving shortly after 1.30pm.

However, it has been clear for some days that Carrick would lose his job after United dropped into the relegation zone following the club’s worst start in 40 years.

When relegation reality kicked in and the dust settled, fans waited for players to confirm their intentions as far as playing in the second tier were concerned. The first two to break cover were inevitably Jarrod Bowen and Tomas Soucek who made their loyalties pretty clear.

Castellanos: All ‘attitude’ and no ‘action’.

#2025. Lewis Hall new insight, excelling in central midfield and as a 10 is intriguing to hear

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Lewis Hall was superb for England in the wins over both Croatia and Spain.

The rest of the world suddenly catching up with what Newcastle United fans have said for a long time.

Lewis Hall is an elite talent and he has been proving that for NUFC across recent seasons.

The lifelong United fan is the best left-back England have, as well as being the most talented in the Premier League.

Very amusing to hear so many people in the media going on like they are the ones who have suddenly ‘discovered’ Lewis Hall.

Somebody who has known Lewis Hall for a very long time is Ed Brand.

Brand worked with him when Hall was an emerging talent at Chelsea.

Former Chelsea Under 18s Head Coach Ed Brand declaring to Sky Sports about Lewis Hall: “What a good kid he is. A lot of the time [with the Chelsea Under 18s] I was playing a 3-4-2-1 formation with 10s…I would put him as a 10 quite a bit because he had always been a central midfield player. If I played a 4-2-3-1 formation then I would play him as one of the 6s or the 8s instead.”

Ed Brand going on to explain how Lewis Hall was then asked to play other roles, left wing-back and eventually left-back: “There were players who were older than Lewis Hall, good players, [so] in certain games where I wanted to keep him in the team, he might have to play at left wing-back even though I knew at that point it was not his favourite position. He was a midfielder. I was going to him [ahead of playing in a match against Tottenham], ‘Look, this is how I will fit you in.’ I just wanted 11 footballers in every position because we wanted to make sure we got on the ball. He started to play there a little bit more, a little bit more, and it just went from there. Now he is seen in most football fans’ eyes as a left back. Whereas I know that growing up, he has always been an attacking player with the ability to get goals and run beyond.”

Brand going on to say: “Lewis Hall was excellent when he was a 10. But people adapt and see your football differently. He is so comfortable at left-back because of where he is used to playing. When you are a player with his ability, used to playing in the centre of the pitch, seeing the game 360, you get moved to full-back, you look at it and think it is easy. He can see everything. Full-backs in the modern game are so important with how they invert inside, they do a lot of stuff infield anyway. With his talent, he excels there. What is so impressive about Lew is how much he has improved upon his defensive side. You cannot play in the Premier League and not be able to defend to a certain level, He will continue to get better the more exposure he gets to that.”

My view for a long time has been that Lewis Hall is such a talented player, he could play anywhere on the pitch and excel.

Ed Brand looking to the future and saying: “He has done brilliantly…[and] in time  he will be one of those England internationals whose name will be one of the first on the sheet. I am biased but I already think there is a big enough case for it.”

#2023. CorSport: RedBird could consider stock market listing of Milan’s new holding company

AC Milan’s new holding company, Milan Sports & Entertainment, could be publicly listed within five years according to a report.

Yesterday, RedBird announced the creation of a new holding company for the AC Milan project, named Milan Sports & Entertainment (MSE). The main goal is to have everything under one roof, from the football team to the new stadium and the NBA Europe project.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

As Cardinale himself said, there will be several new revenue streams that ultimately will benefit the football club, making it possible to invest more money in players and additional infrastructure. In short, it’s a big project and it could get even bigger.

According to Corriere dello Sport this morning, as cited by MilanNews, the launch of MSE proves that RedBird and Cardinale have a long-term plan for the club. A listing on the stock market cannot be ruled out within the next five years either, opening the company up to further investment.

Only two football clubs in Italy are publicly traded, namely Juventus and Lazio, meaning fans can effectively become shareholders. However, it should be noted that these shares rarely come with any real power, used more as a way of raising funds than anything else.

Outside of Italy, clubs like Borussia Dortmund and Manchester United are also publicly listed, so it’s not like Milan would be moving into uncharted territory.

#2020. ‘I would be lying if I said…’ Sean Longstaff very honest on Newcastle United to Leeds United move

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

On 18 July 2025, Sean Longstaff moved from Newcastle United to Leeds United.

The Geordie midfielder had been a mainstay under Eddie Howe and across the Premier League seasons of 2022-23 and 2023-seasons he had featured in 68 of the 76 league games, starting 58 of them.

However, in what proved to be his final Newcastle United season, Sean Longstaff only started eight Premier League matches across the 2024-25 campaign and made 17 mostly brief sub appearances.

In total, Sean Longstaff only played 788 Premier League minutes in that final NUFC season, the equivalent of less than nine full matches of minutes.

So at the age of 27, the midfielder left Newcastle United to get more regular first team football with Leeds United, the Elland Road club paying a reported £12m.

Having turned 29 last month, Sean Longstaff has been reflecting on how things have gone so far in the 16 months since he moved to Leeds United.

The former Newcastle player has only started 11 of the 48 Leeds matches in the Premier League since his move, including only one of 10 this season, spending most of his time watching from the bench…

Sean Longstaff speaking to The Official Leeds United Podcast: “I would be lying if I said it has been the easiest year I’ve ever had. It’s been a tough year. There has probably been times, at home especially, where you are not that nice to be around. Ultimately, I made the decision to come to Leeds. I took my family away from the comforts of being at their home. I have taken a newborn baby away from his grandparents to bring him down here for me to enhance my career. Obviously, at the minute, it’s not gone probably to the perfect plan. But I don’t think life ever does.”

Sean Longstaff is not giving up though: “I take training as serious as possible. Whether that’s the day after a game, whether it is during the week, you have got to train as if you’re going to play. Then ultimately, if you don’t play, that’s not in my control. I can’t control it. All I can control is making sure that I’m fit enough to play when I get a chance, make sure I’m sharp enough, make sure my mentality is right. If I get a chance I want to try and show what I can do, whether that’s for 30 seconds, come on at half-time, or whatever the case may be, I can’t control other people’s decisions, all I can control is the controllables.”

Sean Longstaff comparing and contrasting the two clubs: “It is not until you probably get down here, everyone says Leeds is a massive club, but until you get here, you don’t realise how big it is. I came with an expectation of ‘it’s going to be Newcastle’s this and Leeds is that’….hen you get in, you think ‘oh actually, Leeds is so similar. Apart from the kit, everything else felt exactly the same. Obviously the only difference is me being from Newcastle and not from Leeds, but actually got to know a lot of people from the city and…the way they speak about Leeds is the way I felt about Newcastle. The more you meet people, the more you realise it’s massive.”

#2019. Man United's appointment of Mauricio Pochettino feels like the Glazers are back calling the shots at Old Trafford - with Jim Ratcliffe's henchmen Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox looking like irrelevant also-rans, writes IAN HERBERT

Published: 12:00 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 15:14 EST, 12 November 2026

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada once cited a line from the John Lennon song Beautiful Boy, when relating how an intended 12-month attachment at Barcelona had ended up with him staying there for 13 years. ‘Life is what happens to you while you’re busy making other plans.’

Lennon’s lyric seems far more appropriate to what Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment tells us about Berrada and his dubious grip on United, today.

While Berrada and his director of football Jason Wilcox have been busy making plans for United’s world domination – ‘to create the new history,’ as he described it to the journalist and broadcaster Andy Mitten just five months ago – it seems clear a Glazer family petrified by the shocking descent of their Premier League asset have stepped in to get Pochettino installed.

If it had been left to Berrada and Wilcox, we may have been treated to the sight of Eddie Howe wandering into the Old Trafford madhouse in the next few days. It’s been widely known and reported that Howe was Wilcox’s preference, while Christopher Vivell, director of recruitment, wanted Julian Nagelsmann.

Sources have told us that the Glazers wanted Pochettino and ordered Sir Jim Ratcliffe and his men to fall in line with that. They point to a connection between the Glazers, Pochettino and US billionaire hedge fund owner Ken Griffin.

Griffin was the main financial contributor to the salary which saw Pochettino hired by US Soccer in 2024 and again to that contract extension he signed in August. It was also Griffin, the then youthful founder of Citadel, who provided substantial funds for the Glazers’ takeover of United in 2005. Manchester United deny this, insisting that Pochettino is not a Glazer appointee.

Should Berrada and Wilcox both survive the latest embarrassment – and it would be a travesty if they do, as United pay US Soccer £7.5million in compensation for Pochettino, who would have been out of contract if they’d moved for him in August – then both will be a virtual irrelevance now. Also-rans, bypassed by the latest executive dice roll for United.

Perhaps the TV cameras will pan to them celebrating in the executive seats during some United upturn under Pochettino, weeks or months from now. If so, let it be remembered that it took the influence of others to bend things United’s way.

If Jason Wilcox (left) and Omar Berrada (right) had got their way, we would seemingly have been treated to the sight of Eddie Howe wandering into the Old Trafford madhouse

Instead the Glazers insisted that Mauricio Pochettino (pictured) would have the keys and Sir Jim Ratcliffe and his men fell in line with that

Let us not pretend there’s been any visionary executive oversight from the Glazers. They’ve already rejected Pochettino twice, in favour of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in 2018 and Erik ten Hag four years later.

But sources close to Joel and Avram Glazer, the members of the dynasty who take some interest in their British sports asset, have indicated the brothers have been pushing to get him installed for some weeks.

The Glazers’ connection with US billionaire hedge fund owner Ken Griffin seems significant. Griffin was the main financial contributor to the salary which saw Pochettino hired by US Soccer in 2024 and again to that contract extension he signed in August.

It was also Griffin, the then youthful founder of Citadel, who provided substantial funds for the Glazers’ takeover of United in 2005.

It seems that the Old Trafford hierarchy, like so much about the club, will be skewed from now on. Pochettino does not answer to Berrada and Wilcox in the same way that Ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick have.

He transcends the structure imposed by Ratcliffe, the so-called controller of football operations, and becomes the most powerful man at Old Trafford. The individual on whose vision the futures of Berrada and Wilcox now rest. Should they stay, this is the last chance saloon for them.

United's slump in form this season has been so severe, the club have been forced to dispense with Michael Carrick just six months after giving him a two-year deal

Sources close to Avram (left) and Joel Glazer, the members of the dynasty who take some interest in United, indicate they have been pushing for Pochettino for some weeks

There should be optimism. Pochettino, more than Howe, Julian Nagelsmann, Unai Emery, Antonio Conte and all other available candidates, has the faculty, charisma and fundamental toughness to instil some mettle into United and drag the club from what Ratcliffe and Co have reduced it to. To instil the identity and culture missing for so long.

Time will only tell if he can actually make a go of the most complicated and challenging job in world football, which Ratcliffe has rendered so much harder, by stripping away so many good, essential people from the Old Trafford payroll. That really is a monumental ‘If’.

One United insider spoke for many today when observing: ‘I haven’t got a clue who can make a go of it with the people above them.’

Pochettino will find United no longer command the same spending power, for transfers and wages, as other top clubs, though their name still carries a cachet, if only they can be nimbler and smarter.

He will discover that one of the most godforsaken parts of the operation is the interminable decision-making process: multiple individuals sitting around the table whose opinions must be sought in rule by committee. Some of those who have been shown the door by Ratcliffe consider themselves well out of all that.

The individual United most need now is actually David Gill, the stellar chief executive who left in the same summer as Sir Alex Ferguson, 13 years ago.

Gill would bring a command and intellect way beyond the remotest comprehension of Berrada. He probably wouldn’t want the association with Ineos but nevertheless, United do need to find a proven, world-class chief executive officer. And a sporting director befitting the biggest club in the world.

In that interview with Mitten back in June, Berrada seemed very pleased with himself – sitting on a large sofa in a United meeting room with immaculately bright white adidas trainers and declaring that United had travelled a long way in 12 months.

‘I’m naturally optimistic by nature, although my wife says I should smile more,’ he said. ‘We’ve made some very difficult decisions, but they have put us where we are today.’

It was his 'aspiration’ to ‘make United great again’, he declared. He is a footnote to another unhappy chapter in the modern history of Manchester United, now. The monumental task lies at Pochettino’s door.

#2017. Mavropanos departure claim produces a ‘meh’ response – and here’s why | West Ham News

Had the news filtered through in August, as West Ham prepared to do battle in the Championship, that Dinos Mavropanos had not signed the contract extension put in front of him after relegation, there might have been worry all around.

West Ham had just learned that Axel Disasi wasn’t coming back: The idea of Dinos leaving too would have been downright scary.

At least, going forward, Mavropanos was awesome. Five goals, from anyone, is not a bad return at all in just 15 out of 48 completed games. The lack of clean sheets, though, highlighted West Ham’s defensive vulnerabilities in which Mavropanos was, of course, a key component.

Reports first from Florian Plettenberg at Sky Germany, backed up more recently by KUMB, both claim that Mavropanos in fact did not sign the extension and that with a year and a half left on his West Ham contract, the club are open to selling him if the right offer comes along in January .

Great going forward but back to appearing a more shaky defender

‘Open to selling him’ is very different to ‘going to offload him’ and will presumably be dependent upon bringing a replacement into the club during the winter. West Ham have already parked Jean Clair Todibo in France for a season and so are short of one front line centre back.

Selling Dinos without a replacement isn’t going to be an option. However the willingness of the club to sell if the price is right shows common sense from a financial point of view and, let’s face it, Mavropanos has been no colossus defensively.

In any case there are any number of decent replacements available: Better to grab a solid transfer fee now than lose him for free in a year.

It is a reflection of his more modest defensive performances since Axel Disasi departed that news of his ‘possible’ departure creates little more than a shrug of the shoulders: In fact the back line has been poor for three or four years so this could be the start of something better.

#2016. Sky Sports unveil Newcastle United unfinished transfer business and Matthias Jaissle wish list

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

A new report from Sky Sports claims to unveil the unfinished Newcastle United transfer business.

The broadcaster also naming what they believe the Matthias Jaissle ‘wish list’ to be.

This comes at a point where we are just over six weeks away from the January 2027 transfer window opening.

Sky Sports state: ‘Matthias Jaissle wants to add more goals to his team this January, with a No 9 and a No 10 top of his wish list.’

The report then adding: ‘Matthias Jaissle doesn’t have an out-and-out No 10 in his current squad, despite persisting with the 4-2-3-1 formation since he joined the club in the summer. Joe Willock and Yoane Wissa have both been deployed in that position so far, but neither is natural in that role.’

As for how likely it is that Matthias Jaissle will see a new No 9 and No 10 arriving in January…

Sky Sports reporting: ‘However, the chances of signing players for both positions are slim, unless Newcastle offset that with sales. The winter window is notoriously difficult to operate in, with difference makers being the hardest players to sign. Signing a player for one of those positions is likely to be as good as Newcastle can achieve, given the financial restraints. Jaissle wants to add experience in January, having lost a clutch of experienced players in the summer. This will be his first window to operate in, having arrived late in the summer.’

Sky Sports claiming: ‘Ivan Toney is one striker he admires and would like to sign, having managed him previously with Al Ahli, but he knows it is unlikely to make economic sense for a club trying to invest in younger players with high ceilings.’

The entire Sky Sports report doesn’t even mention the fact that it isn’t Matthias Jaissle who is selecting the signings, with Newcastle United now having given Sporting Director Ross Wilson control of which players are bought and sold.

The Ivan Toney stuff is just lazy nonsense, linking Matthias Jaissle to the striker just because he managed him at Al Ahli.

Ivan Toney is on reported wages of £20m a year and he is Al Ahli’s key striker.

Al Ahli are majority owned by Saudi Arabia PIF, the same as Newcastle United, but the idea they would be willing to sell him to United is laughable, especially at some kind of knockdown price. Even more ridiculous are those fans and people in the media who talk of the possibility of the Saudi club letting Ivan Toney come on loan to NUFC because PIF have majority ownership of both clubs.

The Saudi Arabia PIF, except in very rare cases, treat their business investments on an individual basis and they run independently of each other.

In this case, you only have to look at what happened with Matthias Jaissle to quickly understand how things work.

Al Ahli were furious when Newcastle United took their Head Coach, there was no PIF pulling of the strings.

United had to pay the full £9.5m release clause AND even then Al Ahli messed Newcastle United about further by delaying the paperwork needed to complete the move, meaning Matthias Jaissle wasn’t able to start work with NUFC until 18 days before Newcastle’s Premier League season kicked off.

#2015. Joel Piroe’s admission sums up what most West Ham fans are feeling this season

Not everyone, it seems, is mossing the ‘glitz and glamour’ that participation in the Premier League claims to bring. Higher profiles, more ‘tourist fans’, tougher games, regular pastings by the top six – it is most definitely a double edged sword.

From hundreds of comments on our readers’ section in the summer, West Ham United fans actively looked forward to a season of winning more games in the Championship and hopefully dominating the league after two mentally exhausting seasons at the foot of the Premier League, living with the spectre of relegation seemingly for six months of the year.

The absence of VAR’s infuriating, pointless and often incorrect interference in games has been one of the massive bonuses of Championship football

And of course, the reality of relegation is very different from the perception: Life doesn’t stop when the team you love is booted out of the top flight. And it seems from a players’ perspective, it isn’t all bad either. West Ham’s Joel Piroe, reported by sportwitness.co.uk, has been waxing lyrical as to the benefits of Championship football and how it is tougher than many other European top tiers:

“It’s difficult to explain. Everyone knows the Premier League is considered the best league in the world,” he told VoetbalPrimeur.

“On the other hand, the Championship has the same intensity and the same tempo as the Premier League. It’s much closer to that level than the Eredivisie is.”

…And there is no VAR so it is more rewarding for players and a better, more entertaining spectacle for supporters….. he could have added.

And of course, there’s the proviso that the Championship is all well and good – providing your club gets out of it before financial armageddon condemns it to permanent exile from the top tier.

#2012. Pressure grows for change after Hermansen howler | West Ham News

Whether or not Scott Parker has yet made up his mind about replacing his goalkeeper ahead of Saturday’s resumption of the Championship battle, the highlights reel from last night’s international tie between Denmark and Norway will prove compelling watching for West Ham’s new manager.

Quite possibly, if Parker hasn’t yet decided on a switch, seeing the latest error from his number one ‘keeper may well the tip the scales towards change: Hermansen dwelling too long on the ball and being dispossessed by Martin Odegaard after attempting a step-over inside his own ‘box turned out to be the pivotal moment in the game after Denmark had raced into a two goal lead against their rivals.

Hermansen’s howler proved to be the catalyst for a Norway recovery, scoring three and winning both the game and qualification for the last eight of the UEFA Nations League at the expense of the Danes, finishing second in the group thanks to their superior head-to-head record.

It was the last thing Hermansen needed after his confidence-building performance against Portugal of three nights earlier, when the Dane completed seven saves to keep out his opponents – as West Ham’s web site gleefully told us. I’ll bet they’re silent about his blunder this morning.

The pressure for change between the sticks will only increase now and Areola – or Fin Herrick, frankly –  had better be fit and ready to roll on Saturday afternoon.

#2011. West Ham Receive Double Boost Following Kanté’s Mali Success

West Ham United midfielder Mohamadou Kanté has helped Mali qualify for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations following a 2-0 victory over Rwanda on Tuesday evening. It’s another significant milestone for the young Hammer, who has only just made his senior international debut, and the good news doesn’t end there.

Mali secured qualification with two matches to spare, thanks to goals from Modibo Sagnan and Gaoussou Diarra in Kigali. Kanté came off the bench in the 64th minute, having made his international debut in Friday’s 3-2 victory over the same opponents.

Mali are now guaranteed a place at next summer’s finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. And having discovered precisely when the tournament will take place, I have to say I’m absolutely delighted for Kanté. In fact, it’s double delight as far as I’m concerned.

First and foremost, massive congratulations to Kanté.

Having decided to switch his international allegiance from France to Mali, he’s already playing senior international football and now has a major tournament to look forward to.

It’s a tremendous achievement, particularly when you consider how quickly things have happened for him this season.

Kanté has been one of West Ham’s most impressive players, and his international recognition is thoroughly deserved.

As Claret & Hugh recently reported following his international debut, his performances for the Hammers have now been rewarded with an opportunity to establish himself on the international stage.

But there’s another reason I’m so pleased about this news, and it’s one that makes a massive difference from a West Ham perspective.

I’ve always disliked the fact that the Africa Cup of Nations has so often been plonked directly in the middle of the domestic football season.

As we saw during the last campaign, the losses of both our full-backs, Aaron Wan-Bissaka and El-Hadji Malick Diouf, had a massive impact on West Ham.

Hammers youngster Mohamadou Kanté will be playing in the AFCON

Indeed, I wrote about the problem before their departure for AFCON, when we were facing the prospect of losing two important defenders at a particularly difficult time.

It was hugely frustrating, and I’ve never particularly liked the idea of clubs losing key players for several weeks in the middle of their league campaigns.

But this time, thank goodness, it’s different.

The Confederation of African Football has confirmed that the 2027 tournament will take place from 19 June to 17 July, rather than during the winter months.

That means Kanté can enjoy the experience of representing Mali at a major international tournament without West Ham having to lose him in the middle of the Championship season.

Of course, there’s still the question of whether Kanté will even be at West Ham next summer. Who’s to say he’ll still be at the club next year?

But assuming he is, the timing means Scott Parker won’t suddenly have to manage without one of his most important midfielders for several weeks during a promotion campaign.

#2010. “Don’t talk about it” – Liverpool star criticised for ‘stupid’ decision on international duty

One Liverpool player has been criticised for making a ‘stupid’ decision while representing his country during the international window.

Andoni Iraola was unsure whether Dominik Szoboszlai would partake in Hungary’s UEFA Nations League fixtures against Georgia and Northern Ireland after the midfielder sprained his knee in the Reds’ 3-1 win at Crystal Palace the weekend before last.

The 26-year-old did end up playing the entirety of his country’s 2-0 victory in Tbilisi on Saturday, although he admitted post-match that he felt a twinge during the warm-up and was close to pulling out before opting to play.

Liverpool-focused journalist David Lynch was critical of the midfielder for playing through the pain barrier to the potential detriment of his club, albeit with an acknowledgement that the Reds’ number 8 would feel duty-bound to represent his nation.

The reporter said on Anfield Index’s Media Matters podcast: “I think there’s no other way to describe this than stupid, really. He could have been a little bit smarter in terms of either not playing the game or, if you’re going to play through the pain in that way, maybe don’t talk about it.

“I don’t think Liverpool supporters are going to like it that you’re prioritising to such a degree. Playing for your country is a massive honour, and particularly when you are the captain, I absolutely understand that. I don’t want to play that down at all.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

This is a classic case of multiple parties having their own vested interests at heart. Hungary were obviously pushing for Szoboszlai to play, and he understandably wanted to come through for his country, whereas anyone of an LFC persuasion would much rather he sat it out.

If the midfielder comes through the match against Northern Ireland tomorrow night and is operating at (or close to) 100% for the Reds’ showdown against Manchester United next Sunday, then he’ll feel vindicated in his stance to continue playing.

However, by admitting that he wasn’t fully fit on Saturday, he’s left himself open to condemnation from Liverpool fans (and reporters, in Lynch’s case) who are justifiably asking why he took the risk of potentially aggravating an existing injury and curtailing his involvement for the club which employs him.

That sense of concern is heightened by Iraola’s team entering a frantic period of 11 matches in 40 days to end this calendar year, plus two more in the first five days of 2027. We can’t afford for Szoboszlai to be out of action amid that thankless fixture schedule.

We get that he didn’t want to let his country down unless he was completely unable to play, but he’s now placed added pressure on himself to be available over the coming weeks for Liverpool, and to deliver the kind of consistently top-class performances that he produced last season.

#2009. Origi recalls how Milan tenure turned sour: “We weren’t on the same page”

Divock Origi has discussed what went wrong during his time at AC Milan, from the injuries to the Rossoneri’s decision to exclude him.

Origi joined Milan after the Scudetto season, i.e. the summer of 2022, and the idea was that he would be able to alternate with Olivier Giroud. However, a couple of injuries made his start difficult and it only went downhill from there.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Despite making 36 appearances in his first season, he got just two goals and was thus sent out on loan for the next season, joining Nottingham Forest. One goal and one assist later, he returned to Milan, where it was quickly decided that he was no longer part of the project.

Instead of taking the opportunity to continue his career elsewhere, Origi decided to stay and train on his own. His hefty salary of €4m net (€5.24m gross) frustrated Milan and in December 2025, they finally got the striker to terminate his contract six months earlier than its expiration.

In short, it was a costly deal for Milan and for Origi, the move effectively killed his career. Speaking to the Belgian outlet HLN.be, as cited by MilanPress, the former striker explained what happened and why he then decided to retire (in the summer of 2026).

“At 27, my time at Liverpool was over. Sometimes you need to step out of your comfort zone and take on a new challenge. It’s the only way to grow as a person. AC Milan was a very interesting project.

“Paolo Maldini signed me and I felt he truly believed in me. It’s just that I got injured. Usually, I work on my preparation with my personal trainer, but this time it didn’t work. I lost much of my basic fitness; it was difficult.”

“I don’t take it personally. It was a professional decision. Was I happy about it? Obviously not. But can I understand it? Yes. I was left out of the squad for a while and wasn’t allowed to train with the first team.

“There was the option of joining the youth team. I can’t say too much about some things for contractual reasons… Let’s just say we weren’t on the same page about it. My experience helped me keep a clear head.

“I was convinced that if you have the right intentions, everything will work out for the best in the end.”

“I had options in football, but for me it was also a time when I was starting to think about my future away from the sport. Don’t get me wrong, I’ve always dedicated myself body and soul to football. It was my great passion, ” he stated.

#2008. Jack Grealish APOLOGISES after being dropped for missing training without permission as Everton star continues comeback trail in behind-closed-doors game

Published: 16:18 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 17:13 EST, 12 November 2026

Jack Grealish made his first Everton appearance since being suspended for missing training as he helped a scratch XI beat Derby County 4-1 in a behind closed doors friendly at the Hill Dickinson Stadium.

The 31-year-old continued his reintegration into David Moyes’s squad on Thursday after returning to an individual training programme last Friday.

Grealish was dropped following a breach of club discipline, and apologised to the fans on Thursday evening after an important first step towards returning to the set-up.

'Nice to be back out there with the boys today after a few good days training!' Grealish wrote. 'I want to apologise to the fans (and) everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks.

'I love playing for this club (and) can't wait to be back playing in front of you guys in an Everton shirt.

'See you all soon (blue heart)', Grealish finished, before sharing pictures of himself in action.

Jack Grealish made his first Everton appearance since being suspended for missing training in a behind closed doors friendly at the Hill Dickinson Stadium

Grealish, previously pictured out with a friend, was exiled by Everton but is now set to return to training with the team

Grealish had initially cited illness for missing the club’s trip to Arsenal but after Everton confirmed he had breached discipline, Moyes left him out of the Everton squad for two games against Newcastle United followed by the 3-1 win over Coventry City on Friday.

Thursday’s appearance against Derby was his first in a blue shirt since the 2-0 home defeat to Chelsea on October 17.

Charly Alcaraz scored twice, with 16-year-old Jonathan Nsangou and Christian Norgaard adding the other two in a game that also provided valuable match minutes for Tyler Dibling, Hayden Hackney, Merlin Rohl, Michael Keane, Ainsley Maitland-Niles and goalkeeper Tom King.

Derby had taken the lead through Lars-Jørgen Salvesen.

Moyes has refrained from giving too much away on Grealish’s situation beyond saying: ‘He's unavailable at the moment and we will make a decision with the club when we think that availability comes back.’

He did however confirm the door was still open for his return.

Grealish is trying to rebuild his career on loan at Everton, having fallen out of favour at City despite costing the club £100m in 2021.

Grealish is reported to have gone on consecutive nights out after attending the Pride of Britain Awards on October 19

Grealish, who played a key role helping City win the 2022-23 Treble, will be out of contract at the end of the season.

He scored twice in 22 games for Everton last season during a loan spell which was cut short by injury.

The midfielder returned to the club for a second loan spell this season but had only made six appearances before falling foul of club discipline.

#2007. West Ham’s £18m Castellanos Problem Could Prove Difficult To Solve

Reports originating from Argentine journalist Renzo Pantich have suggested that Taty Castellanos wants to leave West Ham United and has already rejected a lucrative offer from Flamengo in favour of remaining in Europe.

Where in Europe, one may ask – and that’s a question no one knows!

Pantich’s claim has generated plenty of attention, but when you dig beneath the surface, it raises a lot of questions!

The suggestion appears to be that by rejecting Flamengo, Castellanos has demonstrated a desire to leave West Ham while remaining in Europe. Yet that conclusion ignores several important realities.

Firstly, Flamengo are reportedly facing financial difficulties with high transfer debts and sponsorship issues due to the Brazilian government banning football clubs from receiving payments from betting and online casinos.

The Brazilian midfielder reportedly accepted a sizeable wage reduction to join Flamengo. It seems highly unlikely that Castellanos, who is approaching what should be the peak years of his career, would be prepared to make a similar sacrifice.

Flamengo’s interest in the striker is nothing new. The Rio giants admired him during his time at Lazio but were unable to make a deal happen because the finances simply didn’t work. The transfer fee and salary package required were beyond what they were prepared to pay. Indeed, it was suggested at the time the player wanted to remain in Europe – sounds like a déjà vu moment!?

Taty wants to leave but who can realistically afford him?

Lastly, and most importantly, there is no mention of any transfer discussions between West Ham and Flamengo on any news wires.

Nobody doubts the emotional attraction. Castellanos has never hidden his admiration for the Argentine giants, and a move back home would undoubtedly appeal on a personal level. The problem is affordability.

Matching a transfer fee acceptable to West Ham while also covering the striker’s wages would represent a huge financial commitment, even for one of South America’s biggest clubs. As C&H has previously reported, River Plate simply can’t afford the player.

In fact, C&H exclusively revealed that it is West Ham who have been actively exploring ways of finding a buyer for the underperforming forward rather than the player agitating for a move.

Despite accepting a wage reduction following West Ham’s relegation, Castellanos remains on a highly attractive contract. His current deal runs until 2030 and includes a one-year club option.

Even following the Championship wage reduction, he is still earning only marginally less than the reported £48,000 per week he received at Lazio.

Should West Ham return to the Premier League this season and want to activate that extension, Castellanos could still have effectively four years of Premier League-level earnings ahead of him.

At around £77,000 per week, that’s potentially close to £18 million in future wages.

Those are numbers very few clubs outside England’s top flight can realistically match.

There will almost certainly need to be compromise from both sides. West Ham appear keen to move the striker on, while Castellanos may have to accept that replacing those wages elsewhere will be extremely difficult.

For all the speculation, one thing seems clear: finding a buyer may prove considerably harder than finding rumours!

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

#2006. West Ham Exclusive: “Nonsense” Club Source Dismisses Mavropanos Sale Claims

West Ham United have dismissed reports suggesting Konstantinos Mavropanos could be sold during the January transfer window, with a club source telling Claret & Hugh exclusively that the claims are untrue.

Speculation has gathered pace over the last 48 hours following reports that the Hammers would consider offers for the Greek international if a suitable bid arrived. The story has since been picked up by overseas outlets, including Greek broadcaster Novasports, which repeated suggestions that West Ham were open to a January departure.

However, Claret & Hugh has now sought clarification directly from the club, and our source has categorically rejected the suggestion that Mavropanos is available for transfer this winter calling the claims “nonsense”.

The latest speculation centres on Mavropanos reportedly failing to agree a proposed two-year contract extension during the summer, alongside his decision to change representatives and join the ROOF agency.

Those developments have prompted suggestions that West Ham could be prepared to cash in before the defender enters the final stages of his existing contract.

But that is not the position being communicated to Claret & Hugh.

Indeed, we exclusively reported in October that West Ham hold an option to extend Mavropanos’ current agreement, which is otherwise due to expire in 2028.

That provides important context to the latest speculation about his contractual situation.

Dinos being sold in January has been described as nonsense by a West Ham insider

The 28-year-old has been one of West Ham’s most productive players this season, scoring five goals despite operating in central defence.

His performances have attracted interest from elsewhere, with reports from Turkey last month suggesting Beşiktaş were considering a January approach.

However, those reports also indicated that West Ham were reluctant to let the defender leave.

The Hammers are hardly blessed with an abundance of experienced centre-backs, particularly following Axel Disasi’s departure and Jean-Clair Todibo’s loan move to Lens.

And while recent reports have raised questions about Mavropanos’ future, the information supplied to Claret & Hugh today offers a very different picture.

Whatever interest there may be from other clubs, West Ham’s current position is clear.

#2005. Liverpool favourite feared he ‘could have cost’ his country in hard-hitting self-assessment

Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet helped France to victory in the UEFA Nations League on Sunday, but he cut a frustrated figure after their 2-1 win over Turkiye.

The 21-year-old played the full 90 minutes in Bordeaux as Les Bleus finished top of Group A1 to ensure their place in the quarter-finals of the competition, his fourth international appearance after debuting against Belgium in late September.

The youngster has enjoyed an excellent start to his Reds career since moving from Rennes in the summer, but he survived an unenviable moment last night as he carelessly squandered possession in a dangerous area of the pitch before the offside flag came to his rescue.

Speaking after the win for France, Jacquet fronted up to that uncharacteristic error and was grateful that it was ultimately inconsequential for his country.

The Liverpool defender said (via via Made in Foot): “I perhaps preferred my first camp. Tonight, I could have cost the team dearly. Luckily, it was offside! These are little mistakes I need to cut out before I can be satisfied with my performances.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

As magnificent as Jacquet has been in recent weeks, that moment was a reminder that even he can have his lapses, following on from him turning his back for the free kick from which Fenerbahce scored their first goal in the 3-2 win over Liverpool earlier this month.

However, it says a lot about his mentality that he owned up to the mistake for France last night and still isn’t satisfied with his performances, despite his previous displays for Les Bleus drawing praise from some legendary figures of the past.

In the match against Turkiye, the 21-year-old was very tidy in possession and often sought to get his team on the front foot – as reflected below in the statistics from Sofascore – although he might be disappointed at his duel success rate.

Jacquet is still quite young and has had a sharp rise in his career over the past year, and as the stakes get higher in the stratospheric air of playing for Liverpool and France, he’ll learn that the scrutiny which comes with that territory is increasingly unforgiving.

However, his post-match comments after the win for Les Bleus reflect the standards that he expects of himself, and that ever-demanding attitude will serve him very well as he continues his upward trajectory.

One mistake doesn’t detract from what has been a fantastic year on a personal level for the defender, whose ceiling is incredibly high.

#2004. “Grim Reading” West Ham’s London Stadium Financial Problem Just Got Worse

West Ham supporters hoping that relegation to the Championship might bring some financial relief to the London Stadium’s troubled finances may be in for a shock.

The latest accounts for London Stadium LLP, covering the year ending March 2026, reveal an operation still struggling financially, with annual losses of £20.6m, negative net assets of almost £247m and a staggering £243.7m provision for expected losses under its long-term contractual arrangements.

While the figures represent an improvement on the previous year, the stadium remains heavily dependent on financial support from the Greater London Authority and, ultimately, London taxpayers.

But perhaps the most significant revelation for Hammers supporters is the financial impact of relegation.

The biggest concern in the accounts is an onerous contract provision of £243.7m.

In simple terms, this represents the stadium operator’s estimate of future losses from its long-term contractual commitments, principally its concession agreement with West Ham and its access agreement with UK Athletics.

The provision has increased from £206.7m in March 2024 to £241.5m in March 2025 and now £243.7m.

It is not a bill that needs paying immediately, but it highlights the scale of the financial challenge facing the stadium.

The London Stadium financial figures make for grim reading

The accounts explicitly acknowledge the financial consequences of West Ham dropping out of the Premier League.

The stadium’s financial forecasts currently assume the Hammers will return to the top flight after just one season in the Championship.

Should West Ham remain outside the Premier League for another season, the estimated contractual loss provision would increase by a further £2.3m.

That is a sobering admission and demonstrates just how important Premier League football is to the stadium’s financial model.

London Stadium generated revenue of £13.6m during the year, including £4.8m received from West Ham for its use of the ground.

However, this is nowhere near enough to make the operation financially sustainable.

The accounts confirm that the stadium continues to rely on Greater London Authority funding, with a capital contribution of £21.876m received during the year.

The GLA has also provided a letter of support covering at least 12 months from approval of the accounts.

In other words, despite being home to a Premier League football club for almost a decade, the stadium remains dependent on public-sector financial backing.

There was also an interesting development in the long-running financial dispute between West Ham and London Stadium LLP.

The disagreement concerned a payment of approximately £3.6m, plus interest, connected with Daniel Křetínský’s investment in West Ham.

Following a legal battle and an appeal, London Stadium ultimately won the case, with the money released from escrow in April 2026.

The accounts reversed a £3.941m provision previously made for the dispute, helping improve the reported financial result.

There are clearly significant challenges ahead.

The stadium’s financial future depends on West Ham returning to the Premier League, attracting new commercial partnerships, maintaining GLA support and managing its expensive long-term contractual commitments.

The recent departure of chief executive Graham Gilmore after nine years in the role adds another layer of uncertainty, with operations director Darren Raczkowski stepping in as interim chief executive.

For West Ham supporters, there is an uncomfortable irony.

The club’s move to the London Stadium was supposed to provide a modern home and a platform for growth, while delivering a lasting legacy for London.

Yet almost a decade later, the stadium is still losing millions, carries an enormous long-term contractual burden and remains reliant on public money.

And with West Ham now in the Championship, the financial assumptions underpinning the stadium’s future are already under greater pressure.

The big question is how much longer London taxpayers will be expected to support an operation that has yet to demonstrate it can stand on its own two feet.

AC Milan proved that they are willing to spend money on talent in the summer and in January, it’ll seemingly be no different.

There was a shift in the works at Milan in the summer. No longer were the club going to focus solely on buying quantity over quality, hoping for a gem. Instead, they were going to buy quality and so far, it’s largely paying off.

#2002. Archie Gray and Hayden Hackney on Scotland's radar as Sebastien Pocognoli looks to tempt stars away from England

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:44 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 17:53 EST, 12 November 2026

Sebastien Pocognoli has revealed that Scotland are stepping up their efforts to persuade players who are eligible for England to wear Dark Blue.

While the Belgian is content with the group of players at his disposal, he admits he and the SFA are in dialogue with certain individuals who, potentially, could improve the squad.

It’s understood that Tottenham’s Archie Gray and Everton’s Hayden Hackney are among the names with whom there are ongoing discussions ahead of the Euro 2028 qualifiers next year.

Both players have represented England – the country in which they were born – at Under-21 level yet could still switch to Scotland through family connections.

‘I have had direct contact or indirect contact,’ the Belgian admitted when asked about similarly eligible players. ‘When I go to the direct contact, it’s because I feel it’s a first positive approach.

‘Yeah, I’ve done it with many players. I’ll do my best to bring them.’

Scotland boss Pocognoli is keen to add to his options and has spoken to potential new recruits

Under Steve Clarke, Scotland tried to persuade Harvey Barnes to switch allegiance only for the Newcastle player to confirm that he felt English.

Prepared to take each case on its merits, Pocognoli explained: ‘With Barnes it was different. The two other lads (Gray and Hackney) are young lads. It’s a long way. But if you wait too long, it might not be the right moment.

‘In a year’s time, we will see. Right now, we have players in the squad who are performing well.

‘It will always be up to them (current players) to be the priority because we’ve built things and we’ve had time with the ones who are here right now.’

While Pocognoli has previously made it clear that he won’t beg any player to pull on a Scotland shirt, he feels it’s incumbent on him and the SFA to gauge the feelings of players down south who could help his side.

‘We are on it,’ he stressed. ‘We are always proactive in all of these situations.

‘What is very exciting about those two names is that they are young players. That’s interesting.

Archie Gray's dad Andy, uncle Eddie and grandfather Frank all represented Scotland

‘We have to look and manage the situation. But it won’t be a definitive choice from them because we weren’t proactive. That has to be clear. We are proactive.

‘The best way to convince players is to show good football, show them they can come to us, enjoy it and be successful. They have to feel when they leave a top club that they arrive here into top conditions and a top environment.

‘That’s the best publicity we can offer, to show good football. In the end, it’s a human decision, a feeling.

‘I didn’t have that case. With my Italian blood, maybe I wasn’t that good! But I can understand the feeling of what it’s like to have to choose a country, with your background, family, football education and social circle.

‘So, it’s not easy. But it’s always a feeling from inside and I need to feel it. When I feel it, I’ll try to be on it.’

Hayden Hackney has impressed for Everton this season and has played for Scotland Under-21s

Meanwhile, Pocognoli believes a fully fit Kieran Tierney can have a major role to play in his new-look side.

While the preferred systems of his predecessors meant accommodating the Celtic man and Andy Robertson could be a conundrum, the 3-4-3 which the Belgian deploys seems better suited to fielding the pair at the same time.

With Tierney back in contention to face North Macedonia after pulling out of the last squad through injury, the manager said: ‘He will bring a different profile. He has a fantastic left foot and is an experienced player who knows the squad and knows what it means to play for Scotland. It is a big plus. He trained very well this week and is very focused.

‘He can play different positions. He can play left-back, he can play in the back three, as he has in the past. He plays left-back for Celtic, but in some games he has inverted. He can also bring some offensive attributes in the back three. We are lucky to have someone with that profile.

‘It is always a challenge to try to make all the players shine in the best shape possible. We have strong competition on the left side.

‘We have quality players. I will try to find the best balance and make everybody shine. If we can play Kieran and Andy in the same team if they are fit, it is a plus for the team.’

Kieran Tierney has been tipped to have a big impact for Scotland under Pocognoli

Pocognoli is desperate to secure his first victory at Hampden this evening having tasted defeat in his first two home games with Switzerland and Slovenia.

‘I haven’t really experienced Hampden yet and I’d like to,’ he said. ‘I was frustrated in the first game (against the Swiss) because I thought we started quite good in the first 10 minutes.

‘Then we know what happened (red card for Jack Hendry). In the last game, it was just disappointment.

‘It’s important that we play a consistent game and combine a good result with good football. If we play average and win, I’ll be happy with three points.

‘But the process is to play good football as well. It’s important that we excite the fans and we have the players for that. I hope that we deliver what we’ve worked on in the last four days.’

#2001. West Ham Boss Parker Makes January Admission On talkSPORT

West Ham United manager Scott Parker has made it clear that January transfers are not currently at the forefront of his thinking, despite the Hammers’ obvious need to strengthen their squad. Speaking to talkSPORT this morning, Parker suggested that his immediate priority is working with the players already at his disposal.

Asked directly whether West Ham would have money to spend and bring in fresh faces, Parker acknowledged that the January window would be considered if necessary. However, he explained that since arriving at Rush Green, his attention has been almost entirely focused on his players and coaching staff.

Personally, I think he’s absolutely right. Even with the best will in the world, and assuming West Ham bring in some brilliant players in January, there are still nearly two months’ worth of results to fight for with the players currently available. Parker would be absolutely mad to spend too much time concentrating on transfers now.

Speaking during his talkSPORT interview, Parker explained that he had barely spoken to anybody outside his immediate coaching environment since taking charge.

“I’m sure there’ll be an eye in January if need be,” he said, before explaining that his main priority was establishing the habits and principles he wants from his players.

West Ham have a director of football in Nils Koppen, who can deal with precisely this type of thing. There is no reason for Parker to be spending his first few weeks in the job obsessing about transfer targets when the current squad desperately needs coaching.

After all, Claret & Hugh has already revealed that Koppen is working on January recruitment, including an approach to a potential striker signing.

The work is happening behind the scenes, and Parker doesn’t need to be personally involved in every conversation.

Parker can outsource his transfer concerns to Koppen

As Claret & Hugh has already revealed following contact with the football club, January business is being planned.

Every message we’ve received from sources inside the club indicates that promotion back to the Premier League is the overwhelming priority.

Of course, I expect funds to be made available in January. That doesn’t mean West Ham have unlimited money to spend, but the club’s determination to get promoted has been made abundantly clear.

And whilst we’ve previously reported on the financial constraints surrounding January recruitment, that doesn’t mean the club will simply sit on its hands.

But the January transfer window cannot rescue the points we fail to collect in November and December.

That is why Parker is right to concentrate on coaching.

Another interesting aspect of the interview was Parker’s discussion of the mentality required to succeed in the Championship.

He explained that players coming down from the Premier League have often spent months losing football matches, only to find themselves suddenly expected to win almost every week.

That psychological transition, he suggested, can be enormous.

The players clearly have ability, but Parker needs to establish the mentality and habits that allow them to produce it consistently.

If he can do that over the next few weeks, West Ham will be in a considerably stronger position when January arrives.

And if Koppen can then strengthen the areas that need improving, all the better.

For now, though, I’m delighted Parker is concentrating on the job immediately in front of him.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

Jurgen Klopp has proclaimed Florian Wirtz as an ‘extraordinary footballer’ after the Liverpool playmaker’s starring performance for Germany on Monday night.

The 23-year-old scored twice in his country’s 5-0 drubbing of Netherlands in the UEFA Nations League, with his first goal seeing him provide a stunning curled finish from outside the penalty area.

The Reds’ number 7 now has four goals and an assist from his last four international caps, whilst also scoring and assisting in his most recent appearance for his club when they beat Crystal Palace the weekend before last.

In quotes relayed by Sky Germany reporter Patrick Berger on X, the 59-year-old said: “I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer.”

“We’ve also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he’s so vocal. He’s the first pressing player, can press two players without getting tired.”

Klopp’s lofty praise of Wirtz comes just after the 23-year-old’s Liverpool teammate Cody Gakpo hailed his ‘incredible football intelligence‘, and the Reds’ number 7 has been busy confounding his doubters in recent weeks.

He’s been subjected to some heavy criticism since his £100m move from Bayer Leverkusen in June 2025, with Jamie Carragher even calling for him to be dropped from the starting XI, but right now he’s one of the first names on the team sheet for club and country.

In addition to his two goals against Netherlands on Monday, he won three duels, completed 88% of his passes and recorded a 100% dribble success rate (Sofascore), delivering a fine performance throughout the night.

The coach’s comment about the 23-year-old being vocal are also noteworthy – could he develop into a potential future captain for the Reds, provided he stays at Anfield for the long-term?

Our number 7 has copped his share of flak since coming to England, but right now he’s undoubtedly a crucial figure for club and country.

#1998. ‘I am sure…’ – John Aldridge sets Alexander Isak goal tally target for rest of the season

John Aldridge has specified what he feels is a realistic goal tally target for Alexander Isak to try and hit for Liverpool this season.

After an injury-ravaged debut campaign at Anfield in which he netted just four times in 22 appearances, the Swedish marksman has doubled that return in his first 14 outings in 2026/27, scoring seven times in nine Premier League games (Transfermarkt).

Having cost a club-record fee of £125m to sign from Newcastle in the summer of 2025, the 27-year-old has been repaying that outlay with his consistent goalscoring form since August, accounting for 50% of the Reds’ top-flight goal tally for the season so far.

In his latest column for the Liverpool Echo, Aldridge voiced his confidence in Isak to maintain the excellent form that he’s been showing since the start of the campaign.

The former Reds striker wrote: ‘If Liverpool are to have a successful season, then a lot will rest on the goals of Alexander Isak.

‘Now up to eight for the season, the striker just needs to keep getting in the positions and if the chances come, like they have been doing, then more often than not you expect him to finish them off.’

In terms of a goal target for the campaign, Aldridge specified: ‘Having scored eight by this point of the season, I am sure he will be targeting the 20-25-goal tally now.’

(Photo by Justin Setterfield/Getty Images)

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Provided that Isak avoids a recurrence of the injury issues which plagued him last term and extrapolates his current form over a full campaign, there’s no reason why he can’t match Aldridge’s target by the end of May.

With eight goals in 14 matches up to this point, maintaining that return would see Liverpool’s number 9 reach the 20-goal mark in 35 games, and get to 25 goals inside 44 appearances.

As it stands, the Reds will play a bare minimum of 50 matches across the campaign – realistically that number will be closer to 55-60 with progression in the Champions League and domestic cups.

With that in mind, it’s not inconceivable that Isak could get close to 30 goals if he stays fit and in form, although he could be rotated more frequently once Hugo Ekitike returns from injury over the winter, as is currently projected.

Liverpool’s greatest ever goalscorer in Ian Rush rightly said that finding the net is ‘all that matters’ for a centre-forward, and the Sweden international has been doing that in abundance this season.

Barring a cruel twist of fate, we’re sure that the 27-year-old will top the 2o-goal mark by the end of the campaign. At this rate, he could hit it by the end of February.

#1996. Maldini admits career could’ve been different without father and Liedholm: “Liked playing goalkeeper”

Things could’ve been much different for Paolo Maldini at AC Milan without two major figures in his life and career.

Maldini has two faces at Milan, but both remain adored by the fanbase. Firstly, you have the legendary defender, whose number was retired with him, a sign of respect and a chance to honour a career and legacy which surpasses many in the game.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Then, he returned as the sporting director, ending the Scudetto drought. Of course, that story didn’t have an ending as romantic as his playing career, but his legacy lives on. In fact, he may be voted into the Hall of Fame in the very near future.

Speaking to Tuttomercatoweb, via PianetaMilan, Maldini looked at the earliest stages of his career, as well as when he really took off for the Rossoneri.

“When my father took me to try out for AC Milan, I liked playing goalkeeper, but luckily I ended up choosing to be a defender. I played football with my friends in the park and at the youth club: I didn’t feel like I was destined for success at all, and until the day I made my debut, I never thought I could reach the highest levels.

“My dad always told me that the most important thing is to have fun, because if you treat it only as a job, it loses its magic.”

“There’s one person in particular who believed in me and wanted me to play when I was 15: Nils Liedholm, then AC Milan’s coach. He loved showing his faith in young players, and once, during a break, he asked me whether I preferred to play on the right or left. I replied that it was obviously his choice, but it was a gesture that helped me a lot.”

As they say, one change and the rest is history. With Maldini, that was certainly the case.

#1993. Report: How Ronald Araujo, Barcelona and Liverpool feel about prospective permanent transfer

Reports from Spain have hinted that there’s a strong chance of Ronald Araujo signing for Liverpool permanently in 2027.

The Uruguayan defender is on loan at Anfield from Barcelona for this season, with the deal including a purchase option reportedly worth £47m.

The 27-year-old has been one of the Reds’ standout players in the first three months of the campaign, making the right-back berth his own despite playing most of his career at centre-back, and it’s been reported that he and his family are very happy and comfortable on Merseyside.

According to Marca, the Liverpool hierarchy are ‘seriously considering’ taking up the option to sign Araujo permanently and would even be willing to do so immediately, but that clause can’t be activated until the end of this season.

The report adds that ‘everything indicates’ that the defender would be prepared to join the Reds outright if the Merseyside club were to push for a permanent transfer.

Barcelona aren’t considering a return to Camp Nou for the Uruguayan, with an acceptance that they’re powerless to bring him back if LFC were to pay the purchase clause, and it’s deemed ‘highly unlikely’ that he’d revert to his parent club from next summer.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

With the Catalan club not necessarily resigned to their fate, but realising that they don’t hold the balance of power over Araujo, it feels increasingly as though he could become a Liverpool player outright in 2027.

Considering the all-action performances that the Uruguay international has been putting in at Anfield, and that we could lose the experience of Virgil van Dijk and Joe Gomez from our defence if neither sign new contracts, the Reds would be foolish not to try and activate the purchase option.

The 27-year-old seems quite happy to remain on Merseyside for the long-term, by all accounts, and Liverpool would buy him in the knowledge that he’s already proven he can thrive in the Premier League.

If he maintains the performance levels he’s shown so far at LFC throughout a full season, then £47m would seem a very fair outlay for Araujo, who’s helped to stabilise what had been a highly volatile right-back position in our line-up.

It’s frustrating in one sense that we have to wait until the end of the campaign to activate the purchase option, but unless there’s a major plot twist between now and May, we’re confident that a permanent transfer will ultimately be completed and he’ll be a Liverpool player outright in a few months’ time.

#1991. When I overtook Jim Leighton, that was when I started to wind Kenny up about beating his cap tally... ANDY ROBERTSON on going level with Dalglish

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:28 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 18:04 EST, 12 November 2026

It's a story which extols the virtues of loyalty and leadership in the proper sense.

More than anything, though, Andy Robertson’s achievements in football are – and always will be – reminders of what’s possible when a talented individual takes rejection as their motivation to redefine themselves in the eyes of the world.

Even though it’s been told many times before, the tale of the full-back’s determination to bounce back from being shown the door as a teenager by Celtic will never grow old.

Without having the character to overcome such adversity, he would not have been caught in the safety net at Queen’s Park. There would have been no moves to Dundee United and Hull. No Champions League and title-winning medals from his time with Liverpool. No first cap for his country.

In terms of a life lesson for those aspiring footballers who may find themselves in a cul-de-sac in their own careers, it has few equals.

All being well, Robertson will make his 102nd appearance for Scotland against North Macedonia, equalling the record tally of his idol and great friend, Sir Kenny Dalglish.

Andy Robertson will go level with Kenny Dalglish as Scotland's record cap holder on Friday

Both men are proud Glaswegians and Scots who bonded throughout their time together at Anfield. Dalglish would be the first to admit, though, that their respective paths have been distinct.

With a God-given talent so bright it could blind you, Dalglish was a superstar in the making before he wore a Scotland jersey for the first time against Belgium in 1971.

Coming in a friendly in Poland in 2014, Robertson’s first appearance only arrived after those early struggles.

It took huge character for him to even get that far. To add a century more across a dozen years under four different managers is a gargantuan achievement.

Football has a funny habit of throwing up strange co-incidences. Yesterday happened to be 40 years to the day since Dalglish won the last of his caps in a 3-0 win over Luxembourg.

Characteristically, before he took his own walk down memory lane, the man who’ll join him on that mark this evening was at pains to give the Anfield icon his rightful place.

‘It’s not really about me,’ Robertson insisted. ‘For how long the record stood, for starters, for what he (Dalglish) achieved in his career, for the person he is... tomorrow is another reason for our country to honour one of the greatest players that has played a game. He’s definitely the greatest in Scotland.

Dalglish scored 30 goals in his 102 caps and is regarded as Scotland's greatest ever player

‘Obviously, in terms of the number, I will stand side by side with him. But I don’t want people to forget how important this man has been to our country.

‘Because, for me, he was arguably the best player in the world at one time and will always be the greatest in this country, no matter what happens in the future.

‘He’ll always be the first one to do X, Y and Z. I just think that shouldn’t be forgotten.

‘Tomorrow is definitely a reason to do that for Kenny.’

There is, though, still no understating what Robertson has achieved across 12 years. Playing for Scotland wasn’t always the joy that it’s been in more recent times.

‘We get looked after so well off the pitch,’ he offered. ‘That probably wasn’t always the case when I first came in.

‘Under Gordon (Strachan) in my first qualifying campaign, I think I was still young enough to not think too much about it. But then I also remember under Alex McLeish and then the start of Steve Clarke, there was a real disconnect between the country and the players.

‘There wasn’t too much love for the players. We were getting 10,000, 15,000 inside Hampden. That was the most difficult time, especially as captain and being at Liverpool as well.’

He stuck at it and never shirked responsibility. In time he was able to chalk up the numbers because the side steadily improved and broke through the glass ceiling.

Robertson shares a laugh with Nathan Patterson ahead of the visit of North Macedonia

‘Of course, I would be sitting here with a few less caps if we hadn’t been successful,’ he reflected. ‘The fact that we got to two Euros, a World Cup and all the warm-up games and things like that resulted in me having an extra maybe 15 caps.

‘What makes it more special to me is the fact that we’ve managed to achieve things.’

All of this was beyond his wildest dreams at the beginning. A late substitute for Barry Bannan in a friendly in Warsaw on March 5, 2014, he can still hear Gordon Strachan whispering in his ear.

‘He basically said, “Don’t be scared, don’t go into your shell”,’ he recalled. ‘He said, “The reason I’ve picked you is because you’re brave. I see you bombing up and down the pitch for Dundee United”. He said, “Go and be that player”.

‘I always remember the first ball came to me and the words were ringing in my ears. I think I carried it 30 yards forward. It gave me the confidence to just go and try and play exactly the way I was playing under Jackie McNamara.’

Four years later, by then a Liverpool player, Robertson was handed the armband by McLeish following Scott Brown’s retirement.

‘That made me grow up and made me realise what it took to become a leader,’ he reflected. ‘I kind of grew into it. I believe that I became the captain that I wanted to be.’

It was only when he equalled McLeish’s 77 appearances that the prospect of one day equalling or surpassing Dalglish entered his head.

‘I think everyone in the room and everyone who personally knows me well enough knows that personal achievements aren’t really what I focus on,’ he said. ‘But I would lie if I said this wasn’t one that I’ve chased.

Like Dalglish, Robertson is a Liverpool icon having made 378 appearances for the Anfield club

‘I think when I overtook Darren Fletcher (80 caps), when I was in the 80s, it felt like ages for me to get to Jim Leighton (91). Then I thought I’ve only got one more person to go.

‘That’s when I started thinking about it a little bit more, starting to believe that it might happen, started to wind Kenny up a bit more that it was going to happen.

‘I think that was maybe when I realised that this was maybe possible if I got lucky with injuries, if I kept playing for Liverpool.

‘Sat here today, if it happens, it’s something I couldn’t be more proud of. My international career has been everything for me.’

To wear the armband at one international tournament would have been a laudable achievement in itself. To do so three times would have seemed an impossible feat in those difficult early days.

The hunger to repeat the trick at Euro 2028 is as strong as ever.

‘I’ve always kept pushing,’ he said. ‘We’re always trying something new. My wife asked me a similar question last week when we were talking about it. I was going to try and catch Gemma Fay (203 caps), but I think that might be a little bit too far from me...’
